pulls.title: rpc: Optionally print feerates in sat/vb
pulls.body:
Part of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32093

Returning feerates in BTC/kvB it can be very burdensome and is not good practice, as the most widely adopted units are sat/vB.

The RPC affectd by this PR are `getmempoolinfo`, `getnetworkinfo`, `getwalletinfo`, `estimatesmartfee` and `estimaterawfee`.

Because of sub 1sat/vB environment we cannot rely on GetFee() because it internally uses FeeFrac EvaluateFee() function which rounds the values to always return an int. If the `feerate < 1` then it will be rounded to 1 or 0.

For more context or discuss how to migrate also arguments please refer to the open issue https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32093.

pulls.title: fuzz: improve ipc fuzz coverage
pulls.body:
This PR follows up on #35118 and continues the IPC fuzzing work proposed in #23015.

The initial ipc fuzz target exercised normal calls through a libmultiprocess client and server. This PR extends the target with

 - Server side assertions that verify arguments arrive unchanged (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#issuecomment-4452992198 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35118#pullrequestreview-4539477599)
 - A callback call that exercises ipc communication in both directions.
 - Raw capnp requests containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess server.
  - Raw capnp responses containing arbitrary transaction and `UniValue` payloads, which are deserialized by a normal libmultiprocess client.

The raw request and response cases allow the fuzz target to exercise deserialization with data that was not first produced by libmultiprocess serialization.

The ipc setup and callback handling closely follow the existing [`libmultiprocess` tests](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/libmultiprocess/test/mp/test/test.cpp), particularly their use of `EventLoop`, `ProxyClient`, `ProxyServer`, two-way pipes, and `initThreadMap`. 

The transaction and UniValue payload cases exercise the serialization hooks defined in [`common-types.h`](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/master/src/ipc/capnp/common-types.h). 

These files may provide useful background when reviewing the changes.

Generated [coverage report](https://enirox001.github.io/coverage/ipc/) after fuzzing the IPC target for a while using the qa-assets corpus.

pulls.title: crypto: cleanse CSHA512 state in its destructor
pulls.body:
`CSHA512::Finalize()` leaves the digest in the hasher's state and the last block in its buffer, and the class never wipes them. Every `CSHA512` outside tests and benchmarks hashes secret data: in `CCrypter::BytesToKeySHA512AES` the final state holds the key and IV derived from the passphrase, the two hashers in `CHMAC_SHA512` hold BIP32 seed and key material, and the RNG hashers in `random.cpp` hold seed material.

I add a destructor that cleanses both, as `ChaCha20` already does, so each hasher is wiped when it goes out of scope instead of by each caller. Following review, this replaces the one-line cleanse in `crypter.cpp` this PR first proposed. It also makes #36551 unnecessary. A test is impractical, since the object no longer exists once destroyed. I built the tree and ran `test_bitcoin` and `ctest`; both pass, and Core's warning flags report nothing new.

pulls.title: descriptor: Expose key expression parsing
pulls.body:
This PR exposes a utility function to parse and validate a standalone descriptor key expression. 
This is particularly useful in GUI multisig setup flows where the UI accepts a pasted key expression. The GUI can use this parser to validate input, inspect the parsed key,  and apply setup-specific policy i.e. reject private keys, uncompressed keys etc. (Multisig Wizard tracking issue: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35645)

`PubkeyProvider` is the existing internal representation of a parsed key expression. This PR exposes its interface in `descriptor.h` and adds a public `ParsePubkey()` overload that returns the providers produced by the existing parser.

Key changes
- public overload uses P2TR key rules, permitting compressed, x-only, extended, and MuSig key expressions while rejecting uncompressed keys.
- Add `GetOriginInfo()` for retrieving explicitly provided key origin information.

---
Also, while I'm here, I noticed that `musig` parser accepted trailing characters apart from `/`. 
- Add a fix & test to reject unexpected trailing characters after a `musig()` expression

pulls.title: build: Use clang-cl to build on Windows natively
pulls.body:
Building on Windows using Clang instead of the MS compiler may be beneficial, considering the issues with the latter, as outlined in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31456:

>    * non-optimized codegen: [build: remove need to test for endianness #29852 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29852#issuecomment-2049803970)
> 
>    * compile failure: [MSVC 17.12.0 internal compiler error  #31303](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31303)
> 
>    * ~legal, but brittle stdlib: [util: Drop boost posix_time in ParseISO8601DateTime #31391 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31391#issuecomment-2510762011)~
> 
>    * unspecified issue: [refactor: Check translatable format strings at compile-time #31061 (comment)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31061#issuecomment-2531244463)

Additionally, MSVC does not [support](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/assembler/inline/inline-assembler) inline assembly on the ARM and x64 processors.

So this PR:
1. Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/31456 (and addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/14118).
2. Could be an alternative to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/24773.
3. Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36153.
---

Additionally, clang-cl:
1. Produces binaries with [better](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull/1681) performance. For example:

| MSVC, block/s | clang-cl, block/s | benchmark |
|--------------:|------------------:|:----------|
|          7.40 |             11.52 | `ConnectBlockAllEcdsa`
|          7.32 |             11.81 | `ConnectBlockAllSchnorr`
|          7.38 |             11.45 | `ConnectBlockMixedEcdsaSchnorr`
|         91.86 |            143.12 | `DeserializeAndCheckBlockTest`
|        121.46 |            189.04 | `DeserializeBlockTest`

2. Builds faster on the CI:
    - [MSVC](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/13792522864/job/38575846787) - 20m 35s
    - [clang-cl](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/actions/runs/13792522864/job/38575849680) - 12m 43s

pulls.title: Indexes: Harden the flush-error notification invariant
pulls.body:
This is a follow-up to #35714 as it has the two commits of that PR, do not merge or review before that PR

#35714 makes `FlushStateToDisk()` return `state.Error(...)` when `FlushChainstateBlockFile()` fails, relying on the comment `// FlushChainstateBlockFile() already emitted the flush-error notification.`

That invariant holds today, but it is not guaranteed by construction: it depends on every `success = false` branch inside `FlushBlockFile`/`FlushUndoFile` emitting the notification on its own. A future flush source (a new file type, a new error branch) that sets `success = false` **without** notifying would make `FlushStateToDisk()` return an error without `AbortNode()`.

This PR makes sure that **whenever a flush reports failure, the flush-error notification has been emitted**:

- **test: cover FlushBlockFile flush-error notifications**: lower-level `BlockManager` tests (as suggested in the #35714 review) that inject a failure on the block file and on the undo file separately and assert each failure emits `flushError`.
- **blockstorage: encapsulate flush+notify in FlushFile**:  a single `FlushFile()` helper couples the flush and the notification; `FlushBlockFile`/`FlushUndoFile` delegate to it. Behaviour is unchanged.

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block.
Log mismatches and raise a GUI/RPC warning while allowing IBD to continue.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

See https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/configure.html:

> Template specializations for the wchar_t type are required for wide
> character conversion support. Disabling wide character specializations
> may be expedient for initial porting efforts, but builds only a subset
> of what is required by ISO, and is not recommended. By default, this
> option is on. This option can change the library ABI.

pulls.title: descriptor: speed-up `Parse` (xpub/xpriv) in ~30%
pulls.body:
This PR speeds up descriptor parsing, for basically descriptors that use xpub/xpriv, through some targeted improvements (I've been working on fuzz targets for wallet stuff for a while. I've noticed that some of them are slow so I started to work on understanding why and improve what can be improved. The finding came from it):

- Avoid redundant base58 decoding when parsing extended keys (this is the major improvement)

  ParsePubkeyInner unconditionally called both DecodeExtKey() and DecodeExtPubKey(), each running a full DecodeBase58Check (two SHA256 passes over ~111 bytes). A new DecodeExtKeyOrPubKey() function performs a single base58 decode and then checks the prefix, halving the cryptographic work per key. The interfaces of DecodeSecret, DecodeExtKey, and DecodeExtPubKey are also updated to accept string_view instead of const std::string&, eliminating unnecessary string copies in the descriptor parser and allowing DecodeBase58/DecodeBase58Check to use pointer-range iteration instead of strlen.

- Replace O(n) charset lookup with precomputed table

  DescriptorChecksum previously called std::string::find() for every character in the descriptor string, doing up to 96 comparisons per character. This replaces it with a 256-entry precomputed lookup table for O(1) lookups. The benefit scales with descriptor length.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: http: disconnect clients that never finish a request
pulls.body:
The -rpcservertimeout timer only measures inactivity. Every read from a client resets it, so a client that keeps sending bytes without ever completing a request can hold the connection for ever. 

Connection slots are capped by default 16 or by -rpcmaxconnections. Once those slots are taken, the server stops accepting new connections. Because no request ever completes the authentication functions are never hit. 
The impact is low because RPC port binds to localhost by default, so this is a robustness fix rather than a remotely exploitable security issue.

<details> <summary> How to reproduce </summary>

To reproduce: start a node with -rpcmaxconnections=2, open two sockets, and write "GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n" one byte at a time with ten seconds between bytes. bitcoin-cli getblockcount then hangs until one of the (trickling) sockets is closed.

</details>

The fix adds a second deadline next to the idle timer. It is armed on the first byte of a request and expires after -rpcservertimeout (the same value as the idle timer). This timer also does not resets or is extended by later reads. Completing request parsing clears the deadline, so a long-running RPC keeps its connection as before. The deadline is deferred while a worker holds the request, for the same reason the idle timer is. It is restarted while response bytes
are written, because the client cannot start a new request during that window. -rpcservertimeout=0 disables both timers. No new option is added.

Disclaimer this bug is found by utilizing ASTRA. Verified using KIMI 3 and Claude.

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~52 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a six-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: net: stop monitoring select exceptions outside Windows
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
> 
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by ignoring the exceptionSet. Except on Windows, where we instead disconnect if its used.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). But this goes against the spirit of RFC 6093, as documented in the second commit.

pulls.title: http: support unix sockets
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/5029

Accept unix socket paths as options for `-rpcbind=` (server) and `-rpcconnect=` (bitcoin-cli). Options follow the same pattern as `ipcbind`:

- `=unix` is a magic keyword that means `<datadir>/http.sock`
- `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path`
- `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path`

We delete any existing `http.sock` before calling `bind()` and do not clean up at shutdown.

Because access is handled by the filesystem, `-rpcallowip` is ignored for unix sockets and not required at all if we are *only* binding to unix sockets.

Authentication by username/password/cookie is still required.

A new option `--httpunix` is added to the test framework and added to test_runner for `rpc_bind.py` and `interface_http.py` for CI, but (like `--usecli`) most other tests should also pass with that option. When set, bitcoind is started with `-rpcbind=unix...`which overrides `tcp://localhost` entirely. `AuthProxy` has been extended to connect directly to the unix socket.

Try it out!
```
bitcoind -regtest -rpcbind=unix
bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix getbestblockhash
```

Refactored code:

Back in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27375 we added unix socket support but it was isolated to the `Proxy` class. That created a bit of tech debt which we pay off in this PR. Two new classes are implemented:
- `UnixSocketAddr` reflects the `CService` API for generic unix sockets, without bitcoin-p2p-specific attributes
- `SocketAddr` holds a variant of `UnixSocketAddr` and `Cservice` so classes like `Proxy` and `HTTPServer` can operate on an abstract level, with either socket type.
- `CNetAddr` and `CService` are left untouched -- they are somewhat dirty combinations of generic socket classes and bitcoin p2p code, adding unix sockets to those classes wouldn't make sense for bitcoin p2p operations and that's why this design was chosen.

Follow-up suggestions:
- Deduplicate some of the unix socket path resolution code between IPC and HTTP
- On macos the default unix socket buffer size is only ~8k. In the functional tests we have to bump the python client socket buffer up to ~256k or the "throttle" tests will stall on macos. We could apply this socket option on the server side as well, only on macos... requires some bike shedding.
- This option replaces TCP but it does not replace HTTP, there may be a more efficient transport protocol.


Production code and test framework changes designed and authored by my own cranial meatball. Unit tests added by Opus. C++ cleaned up by Fable, security tightened by Kimi-k3 🧠 🤖 🤖 🤖

pulls.title: crypto: plug hardware optimized SHA256 into libsecp256k1's context
pulls.body:
Since https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull//1777 , libsecp256k1 allows an externally provided SHA256 compression function. This PR plug ours in, so it runs on our SHA-NI/ARMv8/SSE4 hardware optimized implementation instead of the libsecp bare internal one.

The biggest gains are at the signing side, not at the verification side.

The first commits restructure how the libsecp context is encapsulated and initialized. `ECC_Context` now properly handles the libsecp context lifecycle and fully behaves as a singleton, getting decoupled from the `key.h/cpp` primitive (which is no longer accessed by upper layers just to init ECC), allowing us to introduce a verification context within the same object, and moving the singleton initialization to `ecc_init.h` which simplifies usage to a single entry point for all users.

pulls.title: kernel: make btck_LogEntry opaque
pulls.body:
Makes `btck_LogEntry` an opaque type with `btck_log_entry_get_*` accessors, instead of a public struct. This allows adding or changing fields without breaking the ABI, and is consistent with ~all other kernel objects. Follow-up to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4207440088. 

I added a benchmark in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...stickies-v:bitcoin:2026-10/kernel-logentry-bench, and found that performance is not meaningfully impacted either way. Some results below.

<details>
<summary>Performance stats</summary>

### Performance

Fields are now converted only when read, at the cost of a library call per field. The [benchmark](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...stickies-v:bitcoin:2026-10/kernel-logentry-bench) measures a kernel log statement up to and including the callback (Apple M4 Pro, static library, `-O2`, median of 2×25 interleaved runs):

| Callback reads | master | PR | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| no fields | 57.4 ns | 55.2 ns | −1.6 to −2.5 ns |
| message only | 57.8 ns | 56.0 ns | −1.4 to −2.0 ns |
| all 9 fields | 57.9 ns | 62.7 ns | +4.8 to +5.4 ns |

Break-even is at 2-3 fields. Either way, the difference is small next to the ~50 ns the log statement costs before the callback, and to what a consumer typically does with the entry (formatting, I/O).
</details>

pulls.title: txgraph: use real intra-cluster dependencies in Trim()
pulls.body:
TxGraph::Trim() builds a rudimentary linearization of the would-be cluster to
decide which transactions to remove. For the dependencies inside each involved
cluster, it did not use the real ones: it added an implicit dependency between
each pair of consecutive transactions in that cluster's linearization. This
makes transactions look dependent when they are not, which can merge
partitions unnecessarily and cause Trim() to remove more transactions than
needed (see #36656).

This PR makes GenericClusterImpl::AppendTrimData() emit the cluster's actual
dependencies (only the reduced parents, since the rest follow by transitivity)
instead of the implicit chain. As a result, several transactions from the same
cluster can be in the heap at the same time. Topological order is still
respected, because a transaction only becomes eligible once all of its
dependencies are met. The related comments in Trim() and in the fuzz test were
updated.

Tests:
- New unit tests `txgraph_trim_no_cascade` and `txgraph_trim_no_overcount` in
  src/test/txgraph_tests.cpp, based on the existing zigzag/flower Trim tests.
- The existing `txgraph` fuzz target exercises Trim() and checks its invariants.

As noted by instagibbs in the issue, this is low priority since Trim() only
runs during reorgs. I have not yet built or run the tests locally, so I'm
opening this as a draft to let CI run.

Fixes #36656.

The destroy method is called automatically by clients using [libmultiprocess](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess), as [sv2-tp](https://github.com/stratum-mining/sv2-tp) does. In the Python tests it also happens when references are destroyed or go out of scope.

pulls.title: ci: cache BSD sdk sources separately
pulls.body:
Sometimes CI jobs need to (re)download *BSD SDK archives, and these downloads can delay or fail the job, as has been happening recently.

The SDKs are currently downloaded and extracted _while building the CI image itself_; this means that when the relevant image-build cache is missed or invalidated, the SDK archives are downloaded again, which is unnecessary.

Instead, cache the BSD SDK archives separately and mount them into the runtime container. Move the BSD SDK setup out of `01_base_install.sh` and run it after the container starts, so it is no longer part of the image build and the BSD SDKs are no longer part of the image build cache/layers.

This means rebuilding the BSD images no longer relies on pulling the SDK archives, reducing reliance and load we have on archive servers in many cases.

While touching 02_run_container.py and adding new paths to it, unify path handling for all caches a bit more.

pulls.title: net: Use exclusive P2P listen sockets on Windows
pulls.body:
on Windows, `SO_REUSEADDR` does not carry over the same semantics as on
POSIX systems. a second socket can set `SO_REUSEADDR` and bind to a
port that is _already in use_ by another process running under
the _same_ user account. this means another local process could bind to
the P2P listen port and receive incoming connections intended for
`bitcoind`.

this matters because the P2P listener is expected to have exclusive
ownership of its address and port. allowing another process to bind to
it could let that process _intercept_ incoming P2P connections. this is
in a similar spirit to #36169, which made the RPC listener exclusive on
Windows.

to fix this, we use `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` for the P2P listen socket on
Windows instead of `SO_REUSEADDR`, while retaining `SO_REUSEADDR` on
other platforms. the added test verifies the expected behaviour by
attempting to bind a second socket to the same port. on Windows, this
fails with `WSAEACCES` (`10013`), which Python exposes as
`PermissionError` (an `OSError` subclass).

references:

- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/using-so-reuseaddr-and-so-exclusiveaddruse
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14388706/how-do-so-reuseaddr-and-so-reuseport-differ/14388707#14388707

pulls.title: fees: return `block_policy` fee rate estimate when `mempool_policy` is not ready
pulls.body:
The first commit of this PR has a minor non breaking API change, it renames the `estimatesmartfee` default estimator option name from "none" to "auto"

----

The mempool fee rate estimator can't always return an estimate:

i)   right after first startup (or after re-syncing through IBD) it hasn't tracked
     enough recent blocks yet;
ii)  the mempool is empty or too sparse to fill the requested block percentile,
     e.g. after a cold restart with persistence off or a missing/corrupt
     mempool.dat.
iii) recent blocks cover too little of the mempool (low coverage); and
iv)  the mempool is still loading.

Previously, case (ii) with a healthy mempool will returned the fee rate
floor (the higher of the minimum relay fee and the current mempool minimum fee).
This can be a significant underestimation, since the now-missing mempool may have
held much higher-feerate transactions. The remaining cases surfaced the mempool
error directly from the combined estimate.

This PR makes the combined estimate (`estimatesmartfee` with
`fee_rate_estimator=none`, the default) fall back to the block policy estimate
whenever the mempool estimator isn't ready, instead of returning the floor or
surfacing the error:

- The mempool estimator now returns an error instead of flooring an unfilled
  percentile, so an empty/sparse mempool is treated like any other not-ready
  state rather than potentially silently underestimating.
- The combined estimate starts from the block policy estimate and only lowers it
  with the mempool estimate when one is available. An error is returned only when
  the block policy estimate itself is unavailable.
- Calling `estimatesmartfee` with `fee_rate_estimator=mempool_policy` explicitly
  still returns the failure.

When the mempool fails to load at startup (persistence off, or a missing/corrupt
mempool.dat), init notifies the estimator, which clears its tracked mined-block
window. Otherwise the estimator would keep a window describing a mempool the node
no longer has; clearing it makes the estimator report insufficient data until the
window refills from the current tip, so the combined estimate falls back to block
policy meanwhile.



This is an alternative to #36095.

pulls.body:
**Problem**: On Windows, `bitcoin.exe` spawns a child process and immediately exits rather than waiting for it to finish. This breaks capturing output and checking exit codes in scripts and tests.

**Solution**: Switch `util::ExecVp` from `_execvp` to `_spawnvp(_P_WAIT)`, which blocks until the child exits and forwards its exit code. Also enable `tool_bitcoin.py` and `interface_gui.py` tests which were skipped due to previous behavior.

This fix requires small changes to `src/util/exec.cpp` and `src/bitcoin.cpp` and there is also an extra commit fixing `errno` message strings on Windows when `ExecVp` fails. Details in commit messages.

pulls.title: test: p2p: check v1 magic bytes only after the full header
pulls.body:
The `p2p_v2_encrypted.py` test can fail in the -- improbable -- case when network reads happen to arrive in smaller chunks (when reading HTTP response from the socket).

Related to #36726 .

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure. In test using sockets on the same host, this is not very likely, but still possible.

The v1 message parser in `P2PConnection` rejected the stream as soon as the first 4 bytes did not match the network magic. bitcoind's `V1Transport::readHeader` waits for the full 24-byte header before checking the magic.

The v2 to v1 downgrade relies on bitcoind's behaviour: an outbound v2 connection is only retried with v1 (`V2Transport::ShouldReconnectV1`) if at least a v1 header's worth of bytes had been sent before the peer disconnected. If the node's first send reaches the test peer in small pieces, the Python peer could disconnect after just 4 bytes, the node would not retry with v1, and p2p_v2_encrypted.py would time out waiting for the reconnection.

This was found -- and can be reproduced -- by using a reproducer patch, that forces all socket sends to use smaller chunking. For the run with the reproducer see #36724 .

The issue is test-code only, the non-test code is correct.

The fix is to match bitcoind by checking the magic only once the full header has been received.

This fix makes the test more robust, even though a failure due to this issue in CI is very unlikely, but not impossible.

pulls.title: test: interface_http: Fix for case when a response doesn't arrive in one recv
pulls.body:
The `interface_http.py` test can fail in the -- improbable -- case when network reads happen to arrive in smaller chunks (when reading HTTP response from the socket).

Related to #36726 .

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure. In test using sockets on the same host, this is not very likely, but still possible.

This tests reads complete HTTP responses, by checking for the HTTP response code texts (`"HTTP/1.1 200"`). In doing so, it implicitly assumes that one HTTP response arrives in one `recv()`. There is no guarantee for this.

This was found -- and can be reproduced -- by using a reproducer patch, that forces all socket sends to use smaller chunking. For the run with the reproducer see #36724 .

The issue is test-code only, the non-test code is correct.

The fix is to follow standard HTTP parsing: read the header until the new line, extract the content length from the header, and read the body of that size. Use repeated receives if needed, until the full response is read.

This fix makes the test more robust, even though a failure due to this issue in CI is very unlikely, but not impossible.

pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: validation: prefetch blocks while connecting
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Connecting a block already on disk requires reading and deserializing it.
Doing this on the validation thread stalls validation and slows reindexing and initial block download.

This is a follow-up to [#35295](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35295), which parallelized input prevout fetching during block connection.

**Fix:** Add a `Chainstate`-owned block fetcher that reads later blocks from disk while the current block is connected.
Start with synchronous 1-block read-ahead, then move reads to an eagerly started worker pool that persists across activations.
Keep caller-provided blocks on the direct path and refill a sliding read-ahead window.
During reorgs, start reading the first sibling while disconnecting the old tip.
Retry speculative failures synchronously when the block is needed.

`-blockfetchthreads=<n>` selects readers per chainstate, with a default of 2 and a cap of 16.
Setting it to 0 disables read-ahead. The window retains up to two blocks per reader, giving 4 by default.
Measurements favor 2 readers with a window of 4 or 8 blocks, so the default uses the smaller window.

**Credit:** The idea comes from [bitcoindev1337](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-08-11#1245429), who had already implemented a similar design and reported comparable results.

pulls.title: test: modernize interface_http and cover more libevent behavior
pulls.body:
This is a follow-up to https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32408 and a new prerequisite for #32061 in response to a few review comments there.

### New test: `check_server_busy_idle_timeout()`

In https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32061#discussion_r2872150590 it is pointed out that the idle timeout set by `-rpcservertimeout` could disconnect a client unfairly if it was the server that was taking too long to process a response. That misbehavior was confirmed and #32061 was updated to match current libevent behavior. This PR asserts the current libevent behavior by adding another test using RPC `waitforblock` past the `-rpcservertimeout` value and then verifying that the HTTP connection is still open.

### Expanded tests: `check_excessive_request_size()` and `check_chunked_transfer()`

https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32061#discussion_r2941508964 made me realize that I was not testing HTTPRequest body size at all, and that headers size was being tested one line at a time but not in total. The libevent server does both things so that behavior is asserted in these expanded tests, and the mechanism in #32061 was improved to match.

### Clean up `interface_http.py`

Since I am extending this test module again I refactored the monolithic test to resemble the current functional test style in the repository, de-duplicating HTTP connection code with a helper class and separating individual test cases into functions.

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: script: clarify implicit signature-cache input requirements
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Signature-cache hashing relies on input requirements that are implicit at its public entry methods.
Inspired by the Elements rangeproof-cache vulnerability behind the recent [Liquid incident](https://blog.blockstream.com/liquid-network-security-incident-assessment) and the [subsequent cache-key fix](https://github.com/ElementsProject/elements/pull/1600), this change clarifies an easy-to-misread hashing pattern: `Write(data, size)` hashes the data bytes without encoding the size.
Bitcoin Core's cache keys already include the signature hash, public key, and signature in separate ECDSA and Schnorr domains.
Bitcoin Core's signature-cache encoding is unambiguous for inputs accepted by its current script checker: a valid ECDSA public key's prefix determines its length, while a Schnorr public key is always 32 bytes, leaving the signature as the remaining suffix.

**Fix:** Extract the common hashing into one typed helper so changes to the ECDSA and Schnorr layouts stay synchronized.
Return the digest by value from the helper and public `ComputeEntry*` methods so callers explicitly initialize the cache entry, where the previous chained `Finalize(entry.begin())` obscured the output assignment.
Document the existing layout and assert the valid ECDSA public-key encoding and 64-byte Schnorr signature requirements.
The serialized bytes and script validity rules are unchanged.

pulls.title: private broadcast: Extra guard against unintended non-private broadcast of private transactions
pulls.body:
Motivation: Reduce the risk of accidental privacy leak happening when broadcasting non-privately a requested transaction that had been previously broadcast privately.

Background: During the initial phase of private broadcast implementation there were unforeseen instances when a private transaction could get broadcast non-privately (see #35032 #35319 #35410 #36309 #36312 #36277 #36330).

Currently known pathways:

- Re-submission through `submitpackage`
- Wallet-rebroadcast (when a private transaction is "picked up" by the wallet, and rebrodcast after 1-2 days)

Note that these are being addressed, but other, currently non-identified pathways cannot be excluded.

Change summary: Add a general, extra safeguard: whenever there is a transaction broadcast request, check if the given transaction has been previously broadcast privately, and if so, refuse to broadcast non-privately.

Transaction relay is not affected, as it should not be affected by private broadcast.  When we receive a previously private-broadcast transaction for the first time (it's not yet in our mempool), we relay it as any other relayed transaction. Behavior is unchanged in this regard.

Notes:

- Prerequisite: This is built on top of #36477, as keeping finished private broadcasts in the queue is a prerequisite for this change to work.
- This proposed change is not an alternative to the use-case specific safeguards, but a complementary one.
- Testing currently uses the two pathways listed above. When they are closed, testing will be more difficult (i.e., it is hard to establish whether non-private broadcast is prevented by the use-case specific or the present generic guard).
- The private broadcast queue is not persisted, it doesn't survive node restarts
- Entries deleted via `abortprivatebroadcast` will be forgotten.

Keeping as Draft, because the prerequisite #36477 is pending.

pulls.title: script: store interpreter stack elements as reference-counted objects
pulls.body:
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures. 

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation 

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes. 

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively. 

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```  

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements. 

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache. 

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs. 

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space. 

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization, while becoming very slow to deserialize.

This PR stores the stack as its serialization in a single allocation (or none if the stack is empty), with a small header holding its size and the offset of the last element. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place, only allowing replacing them entirely. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead. `CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes.

Later commits also introduce stricter checking during deserialization, rejecting the following before fully deserializing:
* Transactions with more inputs/outputs than are possible in a valid transaction.
* Transactions with 0 inputs or 0 outputs (applied in P2P, but not RPC etc. for backward compatibility).
* Transactions/blocks that exceed the 4M weight limit (also only applied in P2P).

The result is a significant reduction in the worst-case time and memory allocations needed for deserialization, both in valid and invalid transactions. With it, the worst-case memory of a valid deserialized block drops from 106.8 MiB to 6.0 MiB. Memory usage during deserialization can temporarily be higher: up to 7.8 MiB for valid blocks, and up to 13.4 MiB for invalid blocks, which can combine a few temporary vector allocations of up to 5 MB each.

Deserialization time and memory of the deserialized block, master → PR. Runtimes are medians in milliseconds. Memory usage is in MiB, and ✕ means rejected at deserialization time. Peak memory refers to the memory during deserialization itself, not persisted in the deserialized `CBlock` object. Numbers over 50 ms, 20 MiB usage, or 100 MiB peak are in **bold**.

| block | gcc | clang | mem | peak mem |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Valid blocks** |
| 1 tx, max 1-byte wit elems | **99.1** → 16.0 | **111.4** → 21.9 | **106.8** → 3.8 | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, max empty wit elems | **279.2** → 18.7 | **293.7** → 25.1 | **91.5** → 3.8 | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout, 1-item wit | 12.33 → 13.39 | 15.00 → 15.43 | 6.7 → 6.0 | 6.7 → 6.0 |
| max txs, 1 txin and 1 txout | 6.43 → 7.04 | 7.87 → 8.30 | 5.8 → 5.6 | 5.8 → 5.6 |
| 1 tx, max txins, 1-elem wit | 4.53 → 4.68 | 5.04 → 5.37 | 4.0 → 2.9 | 4.0 → 2.9 |
| mainnet block 969729 | 5.30 → 5.47 | 5.97 → 6.20 | 3.5 → 2.9 | 3.5 → 2.9 |
| **Invalid blocks** |
| 400k txs, many wit elems, truncated | **84.8** → 16.1 | **95.6** → 21.8 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 12.6 |
| 400k txs, big wit+scriptsig, truncated | **84.0** → 16.1 | **96.0** → 21.7 | ✕ → ✕ | **150.7** → 13.4 |
| 1 tx, 2M 1-byte wit elems | **98.0** → 10.6 | **109.9** → 16.2 | **106.8** → ✕ | **145.9** → 7.8 |
| 1 tx, 4M empty wit elems | **271.0** → 13.4 | **288.9** → 19.6 | **91.6** → ✕ | **182.2** → 7.8 |
| max empty txs | **101.0** → 0.006 | **139.0** → 0.008 | **67.1** → ✕ | 67.1 → 4.8 |
| max txs, 1 txin, 1 txout | 27.6 → 7.3 | 34.5 → 8.5 | **23.4** → ✕ | 23.4 → 6.4 |

So in addition to improving worst cases very significantly, it also provides modest memory usage improvements to the common case. This translates to mildly increasing the effective capacity of memory-bounded data structures that store transactions, like the mempool.

Some notable changes:
* By implementing some checks (for inherently consensus-invalid things) in the deserialization logic, behavior may change. In particular, deserialization errors in P2P cause messages to be dropped/ignored, rather than triggering validation or net processing logic (which may include disconnections and/or inserting into reject filters).
* The rejection of transactions with too many inputs or outputs applies everywhere, including in RPC. That's hopefully a desirable change, but a change in behavior still.
* Random access to the witness stack elements becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$. This is not a problem for any validation logic, but may be relevant for the libbitcoinkernel API which exposes an individual element accessor.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

There are a few possible follow-ups:
* Enforce the 400k WU policy limit during transaction deserialization when active (instead of the 4M WU consensus limit).
* Extend this approach to entire `CTransaction`, allowing all transaction data to be stored packed together in a few allocations (rather than one per input, one per output, one per witness) plus some index structure to access it efficiently. That's a much bigger change, needing abstractions like #35569, but would reduce the maximum memory usage per WU for valid blocks from around 1.5 bytes/WU to 1.1 bytes/WU (compared to ~28 bytes/WU in master).

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: add verify_balance option to importdescriptors
pulls.body:
Another Attempt to fix [#28898](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28898) When importing descriptors, users may provide a timestamp that is too recent. This causes the rescan to miss older payments, leaving the wallet with an incomplete balance. This PR adds an optional `verify_balance` argument to importdescriptors, which is false by default. When enabled, it scans the chainstate UTXO set once for outputs belonging to the wallet’s known scripts. If it finds outputs missing from the wallet, it uses the earliest missing output’s block height to extend the rescan backwards where needed, then scans forward. An earlier requested timestamp is still respected so older transaction history is scanned as well. After rescanning, it compares the wallet’s confirmed mature UTXO outpoints with those collected from the initial chainstate scan. The response includes an info object showing the verification result, UTXO counts and scan details. For example: ```bash bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=restore importdescriptors \ '[{"desc":"","timestamp":"now"}]' true ```
Example response when verification recovers payments: ```json [ { "success": true, "info": { "status": "matched after recovery", "utxo_check": true, "scanned_blocks": 22, "wallet_utxos": 2, "chain_utxos": 2, "scan_start_height": 101, "snapshot_block": "0000000000000001234..01f", "snapshot_height": 122, "recovery_start_height": 101 } } ] ```
If the sets still differ, verification reports `"utxo_check": false` with an error explaining the mismatch. For example, the info object may contain:
Failure Response ```json { "status": "unmatched", "utxo_check": false, "scanned_blocks": 22, "wallet_utxos": 2, "chain_utxos": 1, "scan_start_height": 101, "snapshot_block": "00000000000000001234...01f", "snapshot_height": 122, "recovery_start_height": 101 } ```
Verification failures leave the descriptors imported and keep any transactions already discovered. Required blocks being unavailable is reported explicitly. No automatic retry or fallback rescan is performed. A match verifies the compared UTXO sets; it does not guarantee complete transaction history. Older spent transactions still require an appropriate timestamp or a full rescan. Changes to relevant UTXOs during verification can also cause a mismatch because the final wallet check is compared with the initial chainstate scan. Functional tests cover recovery with recent timestamps, preserving older requested history, mismatches, mempool transactions, invalid requests and unavailable blocks.

pulls.title: txorphanage: bound orphan memory by storing transactions serialized
pulls.body:
The orphanage limits the "usage" of the orphans it stores, per peer and globally, to bound the amount of memory an attacker can make us hold on to. It uses weight as a proxy for that memory, on the assumption that weight is "often higher than the actual memory usage of the transaction".

That assumption does not hold for a deserialized transaction. Every witness stack element is an individually heap-allocated vector, costing its 24-byte slot in the stack vector plus a 32-byte minimum allocation, while only weighing 2WU. A transaction of 199,000 1-byte witness elements weighs 398,247WU (i.e. it is of standard weight, and witness standardness cannot be checked while the inputs are missing), but uses 11.1MB of memory: 28 times what is accounted for it, and one such orphan can be retained per peer.

Rather than change the accounting metric, keep orphans in serialized form, deserializing them again on the paths that hand them back out. Serialized, a transaction's memory usage is bounded by its weight, so the existing weight-based accounting becomes a true upper bound on memory and the worst case is the peers' combined allowances.

Admission, eviction and accounting behavior are unchanged: no transaction that was previously accepted is refused, so orphan resolution (and thus 1p1c package relay) keeps working for standard-weight transactions whose witnesses consist of many small elements, such as BitVM-style transactions.

pulls.title: bench: add  index  benchmarks
pulls.body:
There is a fair amount of work going into the indices at the moment, and no cheap way to tell whether a change actually improves what it set out to improve: checking end to end means a full IBD. The only index benchmark in the tree, `BlockFilterIndexSync`, syncs coinbase-only blocks, so it cannot show anything that scales with what a block contains, and there is none at all for `TxIndex` or `TxoSpenderIndex`.

This adds shared helpers in `src/bench/index_sync_util.{h,cpp}` that build a chain of blocks with chained, validly-signed transactions (~2 inputs and ~2 outputs each, every output paying a distinct key), and on top of them, for txindex, txospenderindex and blockfilterindex:

- `<Index>SyncDisk` / `<Index>SyncMem` — full sync with the index database on the filesystem, and in memory.
- `<Index>Lookup` — one query per indexed key (`FindTx`, `FindSpender`).



How far apart Disk and Mem land depends on the data directory, which defaults to a tmpfs on many Linux systems. Pointing `-testdatadir` at real storage is what makes the difference the cost of the write path:

| Benchmark                           | tmpfs (default) | ext4 via `-testdatadir` |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------: | ----------------------: |
| `TxIndexSyncDisk`                   |          7.0 ms |                 18.1 ms |
| `TxIndexSyncMem`                    |          6.5 ms |                  6.8 ms |
| `TxIndexLookup`                     |         13.4 us |                 13.7 us |
| `TxoSpenderIndexSyncDisk`           |          8.3 ms |                 23.8 ms |
| `TxoSpenderIndexSyncMem`            |          7.8 ms |                  8.1 ms |
| `TxoSpenderIndexLookup`             |         13.8 us |                 14.1 us |
| `BlockFilterIndexSyncRealisticDisk` |         14.7 ms |                 31.0 ms |
| `BlockFilterIndexSyncRealisticMem`  |         13.8 ms |                 17.8 ms |

(this table has data from the old txindex implementation) 

The existing coinbase-only `BlockFilterIndexSync` is left untouched. The whole suite runs in well under a minute.

I have used this on those two pull requests, and in both the interesting number was one the existing benchmark could not produce: #35531 (5-byte siphash keys) trades a 49% smaller index on disk for a lookup regression that grows with index size, and #34489 (batch db writes) cuts `write` syscalls by 91% with CPU unchanged. The numbers are in those threads.




Disclosure: I used claude to help me in some parts, however all code has been verified by me and I ran the bench manually on the scenarios mentioned

Performing a test run with forced chunked send. 

All networking code using sockets must not make assumption about the chunking of the incoming/outgoing data, and should be resilient against any chunking. Normally, the chunking of the sends of the writer dictate the chunking of the receives at the reader, but this is not guaranteed by IP/TCP, intermediate networking elements may change the packet structure.

This branch contains a stress test reproducer. For every socket send, sending is changed to break up data in small chunks. This forcedly changes chunking of the data stream. The goal is to test code for robustness in face of unexpected chunking of the data.

pulls.title: i2p: make a time gap between creating transient sessions and using them
pulls.body:
Connecting to an I2P peer consists of creating a session (the
`SESSION CREATE` command) and then connecting to the peer using that
session (`STREAM CONNECT ID=session_id ...`).

This change is only relevant for transient sessions because when a
persistent session is used it is created once and used for all
connections.

Before this change Bitcoin Core would create the session and use it in
quick succession. That is, the `SESSION CREATE` command would be
immediately followed by `STREAM CONNECT`. This could ease network
activity monitoring by an adversary.

To mitigate that, this change creates sessions upfront without an
immediate demand for new sessions and later uses them. This creates a
time gap between `SESSION CREATE` and `STREAM CONNECT`. Note that there
is always some demand for new I2P connections due to disconnects.

---

Summary of the changes in the code:

* Create the session from the `Session` constructor (send `SESSION CREATE`
  to the I2P SAM proxy). This constructor was only called when transient
  sessions were needed and was immediately followed by `Connect()` which
  would have created the session. So this is a noop change if viewed
  in isolation.

* Every time we try to connect to any peer (not just I2P) create a new
  I2P session, up to a limit (currently 10). This way a bunch of
  sessions are created (`SESSION CREATE`) at times that are decoupled
  from the time when sessions will be used (`STREAM CONNECT`).

* Tweak the code in `CConnman::ConnectNode()` to avoid creating session
  objects while holding `m_unused_i2p_sessions_mutex` because now
  creating `i2p::sam::Session` involves network activity and could take
  a few seconds.

---

Before (note the timestamps):

2025-03-13T09:23:40Z [opencon] [i2p:info] Transient SAM session cd7ea49a7e created
2025-03-13T09:23:43Z [opencon] [i2p] -> STREAM CONNECT ID=cd7ea49a7e DESTINATION=...

2025-03-13T09:23:51Z [opencon] [i2p:info] Transient SAM session cb0956207e created
2025-03-13T09:23:52Z [opencon] [i2p] -> STREAM CONNECT ID=cb0956207e DESTINATION=...

2025-03-13T09:24:04Z [opencon] [i2p:info] Transient SAM session 35ad67f343 created
2025-03-13T09:24:04Z [opencon] [i2p] -> STREAM CONNECT ID=35ad67f343 DESTINATION=...

After:

2025-03-13T17:08:58Z [opencon] [i2p:info] Transient SAM session 16098cd4ea created
2025-03-13T17:09:34Z [opencon] [i2p] -> STREAM CONNECT ID=16098cd4ea DESTINATION=...

2025-03-13T17:09:38Z [opencon] [i2p:info] Transient SAM session 5d209bf1bc created
2025-03-13T17:09:59Z [opencon] [i2p] -> STREAM CONNECT ID=5d209bf1bc DESTINATION=...

2025-03-13T17:09:50Z [opencon] [i2p:info] Transient SAM session e78aa6d2e7 created
2025-03-13T17:12:09Z [opencon] [i2p] -> STREAM CONNECT ID=e78aa6d2e7 DESTINATION=...

---

This was suggested by @eyedeekay some time ago (in 2023 actually) and has been lingering in my TODO since then :eyes:. A further suggestion is to also add a time gap between the activity cease and the closing of the session. For this, when `CNode` is destroyed `CNode::m_i2p_sam_session` would have to be moved elsewhere and destroyed at a later time. cc @zzzi2p

pulls.title: descriptor, rpc, wallet: do not echo key material in error messages
pulls.body:
Some descriptor error messages quote the string the caller sent, and a descriptor can hold a private key. The error then carries the key, or part of it, into places the request may not go: an application's log, an error reporter, a screenshot shared for help.

This PR stops the quoting. A failing key is named by its position, a failing entry of `solving_data.descriptors` by its index, and a function name is quoted only where the parser accepts it. The commit message lists each changed error.

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `key '<key>' is not valid` | `key is not valid` |
| `Multi: key '<key>' is not valid` | `Multi: key 3: key is not valid` |
| `'wpkh(<key>)x' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Unexpected text after the closing ')' of wpkh()` |
| `'<start of a key>(<rest>' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Not a valid descriptor expression` |
| `Unable to parse descriptor '<descriptor>': Missing checksum` | `Unable to parse descriptor at index 1: Missing checksum` |
| `Could not add descriptor '<descriptor>': ...` | the same, quoting the public form of the descriptor |

pulls.title: coins, dbwrapper: remove error catcher, make point-read failures fatal
pulls.body:
**Problem:** #34931 made unreadable coin entries fatal, but `CDBWrapper::Read()` still returns `false` for deserialization failures at every other caller and propagates LevelDB point-read exceptions back to them.
A corrupt txindex point read can consequently fail one RPC while the node continues running.
Chainstate also retains `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher` as a separate view layer solely to invoke its fatal-error callback.

**Fix:** Make LevelDB point-read and typed deserialization failures fatal in `CDBWrapper`, after logging the database path and error and invoking the fatal-notification callback when one was provided.
Missing keys still return `false`, database-open failures keep using the existing initialization paths, and iterator decoding remains unchanged.
Pass the callback at construction for chainstate, the block-index database, and optional index databases, remove `CCoinsViewErrorCatcher`, keep `HaveCoin()` on the cache view that owns its caching behavior, and mark coin-view lookups `noexcept`.

pulls.title: psbt: classify missing Taproot script-path signatures as signer
pulls.body:
This is my first Bitcoin Core PR.

I originally reported #36035 after running into this while experimenting with Taproot 2-of-3 multisig on Signet. After reporting it, I wanted to see whether I could actually trace the problem in the source code and try to fix it myself.

I used ChatGPT Pro as a tool to help me navigate the codebase, understand the PSBT analysis/signing flow, and test different hypotheses. I followed the changes myself, built Bitcoin Core locally, and ran the tests rather than just submitting generated code.

The issue appears to come from the Taproot script-path signing path not recording a missing signature in missing_sigs when a Schnorr signature is not available. AnalyzePSBT() uses missing_sigs to decide whether the next role should be signer. Without it, the PSBT was classified as updater, which is also why the GUI displayed “Transaction is missing some information about inputs.”

My first attempt at the fix did not work. The regression test still returned updater, which led me to notice that SignMuSig2() can return successfully without actually producing a Taproot script-path signature. I adjusted the change so that, after the Schnorr/MuSig2 attempts, a missing signature is recorded when no script-path signature was produced.

I also added a regression test that checks that this Taproot script-path case is classified as signer.

I tested the change locally with:

test/functional/rpc_psbt.py
test/functional/wallet_musig.py
test_bitcoin --run_test=psbt_tests
test_bitcoin --run_test=miniscript_tests
git diff --check

All of these passed with the current patch.

This appears to fix the behavior I reported in #36035. Since this is my first contribution, feedback on both the approach and the implementation is very welcome.

Fixes #36035

pulls.title: refactor: make script Solver's often-unused solutions parameter optional
pulls.body:
### Summary
Many callsites only need to determine the script type and don't use the parsed solutions.
Previously, these callers still incurred the cost of allocating and populating a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`.

### Fix
Changing `Solver` signature from reference to nullable pointer parameter with `nullptr` default allows calling the method for its result only. Note that we can't call `std::optional` here because that would copy the values but we need the result to be provided from the outside to avoid the copies.
Inside the `Solver` we guard all accesses to the solutions parameter.
Callsites were changed to pass `&solutions` only when they need the data and removed when we don't.

### Origin & Alternative
This was originally discovered in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/32279/files#diff-060e8fd790fc1c3e18c64327a7395bb5b2d6d57db9792cc666bd8d7354a40c0bR1154-R1159 where we needed to test the allocation characteristics of different templates.
This supersedes the vector reuse optimization approach in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33645#issuecomment-3436715527 by addressing the problem more fundamentally - avoiding unnecessary work entirely rather than optimizing it. The author of the different change was added as a coauthor.

pulls.title: validation: Separate check-only version of ConnectBlock
pulls.body:
This is a small code-hygiene refactor to `ConnectBlock` method.

Problem:  In the "check-only" mode of `ConnectBlock` the mutability of the `CBlockIndex` parameter is inconsistent with the semantics. In the default operation, `ConnectBlock` changes the provided `CBlockIndex`. However, it has a special "check-only" mode, where the provided chain is not changed. This mode is used from only one call site (`TestBlockValidity`), and is signaled by the `fJustCheck = true` flag.

Solution:  Provide two versions of `ConnectBlock`: one with mutable chain and one "check-only" with const chain (`TestConnectBlock`). There is no need for the `fJustCheck` flag. Both reuse the same internal implementation. The non-public implementation method still uses the flag, but its usage has been reduced.

Benefits:
- The mutability of the `pindex` parameter is in sync with the semantics
- One less feature flag (`fJustCheck`) on the public methods
- Calling "check-only" mode is smoother, creating a dummy mutable `CBlockIndex` is now unnecessary

Additional details:
- This has been triggered by #35187, there is also a new usage of "check-only" `ConnectBlock`, with dummy `CBlockIndex`.
- The "check-only" mode was introduced as early as 2012 (3cd01fdf0e540c4e06cd27b6c0d6b6abc00767d1).
- No behavior change (pure refactor).
- Some internal variables (`blockundo`,  `nInputs`, `nSigOpsCost`) are now outputs of the internal method, and used in the default outer method (`ConnectBlock`).
- `SetBestBlock` has been moved to the outer `ConnectBlock`. It was also present in the special genesis block early return, this is preserved.
- The tracepoints are in the outer methods
- Timing is present both in the inner method (logs) and the outer methods (logs, tracepoint)

its reach. A dedicated wallet interface makes it available for multisig setup.
Alongside the addhdkey interface, this lets the GUI add an HD key and derive a
shareable xpub from it. Tracked as the deriveHDKey item in #35645.

Key changes:
- Move the key selection and derivation logic from the RPC into CWallet::DeriveHDKey, including the wallet and argument checks.
- Have the RPC call CWallet::DeriveHDKey and translate its WalletError using HandleWalletErrorCode.
- Add interfaces::Wallet::deriveHDKey, which returns the derived xpub and key origin. Private materials are not exposed through the interface.
- Add interface tests for derivation and error forwarding. Update the functional tests for the changed error codes and unlock message.

pulls.title: mining: replace interrupt methods with cancellation arguments
pulls.body:
**Depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#342. Only the last commit belongs to this PR.**

---

The blocking methods (`waitTipChanged`, `createNewBlock`, and `BlockTemplate::waitNext`) currently rely on `interrupt()`/`interruptWait()` to cancel them when they are in progress (#33676, #34184). With request cancellation support in libmultiprocess (bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#342), this is no longer needed.

This PR adds `CancelArg` arguments to those blocking methods to register a callback that runs on cancellation and deprecates the interrupt methods. Registering returns a `CancelGuard` that unregisters the callback when destroyed, so the event loop can't run it after the wrapped method goes out of scope.

In the capnp schema, use the `Proxy.extraParam` annotation for the C++ `CancelArg` parameter and the `Cxx.allowCancellation` annotation to enable request cancellation at the RPC layer.

The `CustomBuildExtraParam`/`CustomReadExtraParam` overloads for `CancelArg` live in `ipc/capnp/common-types.h`, following the reference implementation in the libmultiprocess PR. The client side wraps the request in a `kj::Canceler` and throws `InterruptException` when canceled, while the server side registers the method's callback with the request's server context, where the event loop runs it on cancellation.

In tests, update miner_tests to cancel `waitNext()` from another thread, and interface_ipc_mining.py to drop the response promise. Also add `drop_promise()` to ipc_util.py to abandon capnp promises, and a cancelable `waitCancel` method to the ipc_tests `FooInterface` to exercise both the client and server hooks.

Additional note: this is the Bitcoin Core side of approach 4 in #33575.

pulls.title: test: deduplicate reorg test code
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #32587. 

`trigger_reorg()` was copy-pasted across several functional tests. This moves it into `blocktools.py`, together with the fork construction, as two helpers: `create_empty_fork()` and `trigger_reorg()`. 

The remaining tests that still simulated reorgs with the `invalidateblock` RPC are converted to use them, since `invalidateblock` takes a different codepath than a reorg caused by a competing chain arriving.

pulls.title: test: fix coinbases built on arbitrary parents
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Test helpers that attach active-tip templates to arbitrary parents retain the template's subsidy.
Existing reorg tests can underpay without failing, while a fork crossing a halving can overpay and fail with `bad-cb-amount`.
Bare height scripts at heights 1 through 16 also fail with `bad-cb-length`.

**Fix:** Share parent-dependent reconstruction between `BuildChain()` and `MinerTestingSetup::Block()`, deriving difficulty and coinbase fields from the actual parent.
Pad rebuilt coinbase input scripts and require coinbase-only templates so recalculating the subsidy cannot discard transaction fees.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.

pulls.title: net: validate Tor onion service replies and cached keys
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A node creates its onion service through Tor's control protocol and caches the returned `PrivateKey` value for reconnects.
Tor reply parsing unescapes quoted values, so a control endpoint can return a value containing a line break or space.
On reconnect, the node inserts that value unquoted into an `ADD_ONION` command.
CRLF frames the remainder as a separate command, while a space adds further arguments.
An unprivileged local process can exploit this by impersonating the default loopback endpoint while Tor is unavailable, seeding the cache, and releasing the port before Tor is available again.
A compromised operator-configured endpoint can return the same malicious value.
The reply handler also continues after receiving an invalid service ID, logging it and caching the key before attempting to advertise the invalid address.
A later reply without a service ID can reuse an ID left by an earlier reply.

**Fix:** This PR validates the returned service ID as a Tor v3 onion address before logging it, caching the key, or advertising the service.
Each reply must provide its own service ID, and reply fields stay local until validation succeeds.
Key validation accepts `NEW:ED25519-V3` or an `ED25519-V3` key whose Base64 payload decodes to 64 bytes.
Returned keys are validated before adoption or caching, and cached keys are validated before reuse.
A malformed cached key leaves the onion service unavailable until the operator removes the file and restarts the node. It cannot inject another command or argument.

pulls.title: doc: clarify RPC addnode 'add' vs 'onetry' connection limits
pulls.body:
Clarifies the `addnode` RPC help on the separate limits for `add` and `onetry`: `add` entries are capped by `MAX_ADDNODE_CONNECTIONS`, `onetry` connections are not.

Also fixes `-netinfo`: the manual peer count is `uint8_t` while the other counts are `uint16_t`, so it wraps at 256. This is reachable via `addnode onetry`, which is not subject to the `MAX_ADDNODE_CONNECTIONS` cap.

pulls.title: node: don't abort on invalid -dbcache in settings.json
pulls.body:
`LogOversizedDbCache` (added in #33333) is `noexcept`, but it reads `-dbcache` through `CalculateDbCacheBytes` -> `GetIntArg`. `GetIntArg` throws when settings.json has a number that isn't an integer or doesn't fit in int64, e.g. `{"dbcache": 4096.5}`. The exception hits the `noexcept` boundary and bitcoind aborts during startup:

```
libc++abi: terminating due to uncaught exception of type std::runtime_error: JSON integer out of range
```

This removes `noexcept`. The exception now reaches the handler in `AppInit`, and the node exits with status 1 and an error message instead of aborting:

```
EXCEPTION: St13runtime_error
JSON integer out of range
bitcoin in AppInit()
```

The added case in `feature_settings.py` writes `{"dbcache": 4096.5}` to settings.json and checks that startup fails with that message from `AppInit`.

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.
