pulls.title: net: require a dedicated bind for automatic Tor
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When the automatic onion service has no dedicated `-bind=<addr>=onion`, Tor forwards incoming connections to the first normal P2P bind. A wildcard onion bind also fails to identify incoming Tor connections. In either case, network classification is incorrect and Tor peers may inherit permissions granted to the Tor daemon's IP address.

**Fix:** Refuse startup when `-listenonion` is enabled and an explicit `-bind` configuration lacks a dedicated, non-wildcard onion bind or includes a wildcard onion bind, following [the recommendation in #34892](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34892#issuecomment-5541662236). Users should add a specific `-bind=<addr>=onion` or set `-listenonion=0`.

Because `-listenonion` is enabled by default when listening, existing configurations with only a normal `-bind` must also be updated. Nodes without explicit `-bind` options retain the default dedicated onion listener.

pulls.title: test: allow 3 bytes of fee overestimate in assert_fee_amount
pulls.body:
The wallet sizes a transaction assuming a 71-byte low-R ECDSA signature. A signature whose r or s has leading zero bytes is shorter, so the fee can cover a few bytes more than the signed transaction needs. In #36394 the wallet estimated 219 bytes and paid 438 sat at 2 sat/vB, but the signed transaction was 216 bytes: the signature was 3 bytes short. That happens about once in 4 million signatures. `assert_fee_amount` allows only 2 bytes of overestimate, so the test failed.

I raise the allowance to 3 bytes, which makes the failure about 200 times rarer. The check that the fee is not too low is unchanged. @maflcko suggested 3 bytes in #24151 and #25164.

Fixes #36394.

*Made with my usual tools: a computer, the Internet and an LLM. The mistakes, as usual, are all mine.*

pulls.title: build: pass hardening flags to secp256k1
pulls.body:
The secp256k1 subtree is built without our hardening flags: they are on `core_interface`, which the subtree does not use, so unless the compiler enables them by default its objects miss FORTIFY, the stack protector, stack clash protection and control flow protection. On aarch64 Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15, the three secp256k1 objects are the only ones in the build tree without the control flow property, so master's `bitcoind` has no `AArch64 feature` note.

This PR moves the flags back to a `hardening_interface` library, which `core_interface` links (reverting 77e553ab6a), and `cmake/secp256k1.cmake` passes the subtree those its C compiler accepts. The same build then shows `AArch64 feature: BTI, PAC, GCS` on `bitcoind`. The depends libraries still lack `-fcf-protection` (#30677, #30685).

pulls.title: coins: warn of low disk space before chainstate compaction
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Full chainstate compaction can temporarily require nearly another copy of the database before old files are deleted.

**Fix:** Log automatic full compaction start and finish at info level. Before starting, check the free space on the chainstate filesystem, and if it is below `m_assumed_chain_state_size`, log a warning and skip this compaction. Skipping avoids the temporary extra disk use but leaves obsolete data taking up space.

Fixes #36585

pulls.title: log: escape C1 control characters in messages
pulls.body:
The log escapes control characters so that a message cannot drive the terminal it is printed on, but it lets through the UTF-8 form of the C1 controls U+0080 to U+009F. VTE, the library behind GNOME Terminal and others, decodes these as CSI, OSC, DCS and the rest, like their `ESC [`, `ESC ]` and `ESC P` forms.

I escape the two-byte sequences 0xC2 0x80 to 0xC2 0x9F as `\xc2\x9b` and so on. Since 0xC2 is never a continuation byte, this needs no UTF-8 decoder, and all other non-ASCII text still passes untouched, as asked in #17095 and #35833. Single bytes 0x80 to 0x9F stay as they are, since they occur inside valid UTF-8. The new cases in `test_LogEscapeMessage` fail on master and pass with the change.

pulls.title: fuzz: Add a target that feeds arbitrary bytes to V2Transport
pulls.body:
No fuzz target feeds V2Transport bytes that an honest peer would not send past the v2 key exchange. I add p2p_transport_v2_receive. It knows the transport's keys, builds the input from arbitrary bytes and from parts of a valid handshake (the peer key, garbage, the terminator, encrypted packets that may be corrupted, and runs of empty decoys that force a rekey), and feeds it in pieces of arbitrary size. Once the transport reports v2, it checks that its session id matches the peer's.

It reaches the v2 receive states and their failures, except the fallback to v1 and the wrong-magic disconnect, which need a v1 `version` header at the start of the stream; `p2p_transport_bidirectional_v1v2` reaches the first. 15 minutes with libFuzzer, ASan and UBSan found no crash.

pulls.title: test: cover unsatisfiable mining timestamp
pulls.body:
This PR adds test coverage for what happens in the (extremely unlikely) event that the miner can't satisfy the constraints. This is inspired by the recently added timewarp-protection and Murch-Zawy rules (for the miner, not for consensus, see #30681 and #35949), but this is a pre-existing issue. It is not made worse by these rules.

The test has an attacker mine 6 blocks, which set MTP at the victim's future-time limit. It calls `getblocktemplate` and the equivalent IPC method, which both fail. It then moves mock time one second forward, and demonstrates mining works again (and we don't drop the IPC connection).

This (impractical) attack can be done at any height, be we illustrate it for blocks 142, 143 and 0 of a retarget period, to clarify that the timewarp-protection and Murch-Zawy rules do not matter.

The test was added to `ipc_mining.py`, to avoid having to add IPC support to `mining_basic.py`. Mining coverage is currently split between various test files and not always mirrored between RPC and IPC. A followup could unify these, while still skipping the IPC side when that's not compiled.

A few refactor commits to prepare:

- fix incorrect name: `REGTEST_RETARGET_PERIOD` -> `HALVING_INTERVAL`
- drop `REGTEST_` prefix from `REGTEST_N_BITS` and `REGTEST_TARGET` (consistent with `HALVING_INTERVAL`, `DIFFICULTY_ADJUSTMENT_INTERVAL` and `TIME_GENESIS_BLOCK`).
- move `DIFFICULTY_ADJUSTMENT_INTERVAL` to the framework

The last commit picks up a Murch-Zawy followup suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35949#discussion_r3944011135 and takes advantage of our refactor, but is otherwise unrelated.

pulls.title: kernel: document the import_blocks abort
pulls.body: A second btck_chainstate_manager_import_blocks call on the same chainstate manager, while one is in progress, aborts the process, and the kernel header does not say so. I document it. The abort is the assert in ImportingNow in node/blockstorage.cpp, which I keep.

pulls.title: rpc: reset id and version per batch element
pulls.body:
In a JSON-RPC batch, an element that is not an object gets an error reply with the id and version of the element before it.

`ExecuteHTTPRPC` uses one request object for the whole batch. `parse()` throws on a non-object before it resets `id` and `m_json_version`. For `[{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"getblockcount","id":"X"}, 2]` the reply has two objects with `"id":"X"`, one with a result and one with an error. If the first element is a notification, the error is dropped. I reset both fields at the top of `parse()`, so the error is the one the first element of a batch already gets. The new case in `interface_rpc.py` fails on master and passes with this change.

pulls.title: mempool: recalculate stale BIP68 lockpoints in removeForReorg
pulls.body:
When a reorg lowers the tip, `removeForReorg` can evict BIP68 transactions that are still valid at the new tip, together with all their descendants.

A transaction that spends an unconfirmed parent gets its lockpoints cached with that input at height tip+1. After `invalidateblock`, `TestLockPointValidity` can still pass on those cached lockpoints (always when every input was unconfirmed, since `maxInputBlock` is then genesis; and with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs when the confirmed input's block survives), so `CheckSequenceLocksAtTip` is evaluated against stale values and the transaction is removed.

The fix, suggested by ismaelsadeeq, is to never evict on cached lockpoints alone: if they are not valid at the new tip, or the cached sequence-lock check fails, recalculate them with `CalculateLockPointsAtTip` and evict only if the fresh result also fails. This covers height-based and time-based locks alike, at the cost of some recalculations that turn out to be unnecessary.

`mempool_reorg_bip68_stale_lockpoints.py` covers four cases across a reorg: a BIP68-disabled child, a BIP68-enabled child of an unconfirmed parent, a child with mixed confirmed and unconfirmed inputs, and a time-based zero lock where the reorg lowers the median time past (test by Bicaru20). The test fails on master, and the mixed-input case also fails on the earlier genesis-only version of this fix.

Reproducer for unpatched nodes:
https://gist.github.com/javierpmateos/c55d365973adbf488a852dc5e0b77dec

Same class of issue fixed for TRUC in #33504.

Closes #35007

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

pulls.title: wallet: fill PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB
pulls.body:
Closes #27583.

`PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` already serializes, deserializes and merges when PSBTs are combined. Nothing writes it, so a PSBT produced by the wallet never carries it, and a signer that only has the file cannot rebuild the multisig from it. Today Specter [fills the field itself](https://github.com/cryptoadvance/specter-desktop/blob/8843e2f0640a9adc129f9ab6afe5ecb9632e7c5b/src/cryptoadvance/specter/wallet/wallet.py#L1866-L1881) after getting the PSBT from Core.

<details><summary>Before and after with the BitBox02 and Trezor simulators</summary>

A 2-of-3 `wsh(sortedmulti(...))` on regtest with the simulator as one co-signer, signed through HWI 3.2.0. The "before" file is the same PSBT with its `PSBT_GLOBAL_XPUB` records removed, so nothing else differs.

| | without the field | with the field |
|---|---|---|
| BitBox02 | refuses, `This BitBox02 is not one of the cosigners` | signs |
| Trezor T | signs, co-signer nodes sent with zeroed chain codes and no derivation paths | signs, nodes sent with the real chain codes and paths |

What `parse_multisig` hands the Trezor for the change output:

```
without: global xpubs=0  zeroed chain codes=3/3  depths=[0, 0, 0]  paths=[[], [], []]
with   : global xpubs=3  zeroed chain codes=0/3  depths=[4, 4, 4]  paths=[[1, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0]]
```

</details>

A new `Descriptor` accessor returns the extended keys a descriptor is built from, and `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::FillPSBT` writes those of every descriptor with an input or an output in the PSBT. That covers `walletcreatefundedpsbt`, `walletprocesspsbt`, `send`, `sendall`, `psbtbumpfee` and the GUI send dialog, which all go through `CWallet::FillPSBT`.

Only the keys BIP 174 allows are added, the ones that derive, through unhardened steps alone, a key the PSBT gives a derivation path for. So a key expression ending in `/*h` adds nothing.

Whoever holds a PSBT from the wallet can now derive the addresses of the descriptors it uses. Setting `bip32derivs` to false in `walletcreatefundedpsbt` or `walletprocesspsbt` leaves the field out, along with the derivation paths.

`descriptorprocesspsbt` is left out, since it signs from the descriptors it is given without going through the wallet, and I intend to cover it as a follow-up.

pulls.title: test: fix TaprootSignatureMsg default codeseparator_pos
pulls.body:
`TaprootSignatureMsg` defaults `codeseparator_pos` to `-1` and serializes it with `.to_bytes(4, "little", signed=False)`, so any `scriptpath=True` call that relies on the default raises `OverflowError`. 81e5c8385b made the encoding unsigned and left this default at `-1`. The only in-tree scriptpath caller passes `codeseparator_pos` explicitly, so CI does not hit it.

Make the default `None`, like `leaf_script`, and assert that scriptpath callers pass it. A call that omits it now fails with a clear message.

pulls.title: crypto: cleanse HMAC hasher state and MuSig2 signing keypair
pulls.body:
`CHMAC_SHA256` and `CHMAC_SHA512` do not wipe their two hasher objects when they are destroyed. After `Finalize()` these still hold the HMAC output and the last bytes of the message, so `CExtKey::SetSeed()` leaves the seed and the master key behind, and `BIP32Hash()` for a hardened child leaves the parent private key. `CreateMuSig2PartialSig()` also leaves a `secp256k1_keypair`, which contains the secret key, on the stack.

I add destructors to both HMAC classes that `memory_cleanse()` the two hashers, following #35254, which cleansed `rkey` and `temp` in the same files. The MuSig2 keypair now comes from `CKey::ComputeKeyPair()`, which keeps it in secure memory. I checked with a small program, built from these files, that the seed and key bytes are in the HMAC object after `Finalize()` and gone after its destructor.

pulls.title: test: reduce hash mod n for RFC6979 nonce
pulls.body:
`sign_ecdsa(..., rfc6979=True)` in the test framework derives the nonce from the raw message hash. RFC6979 section 2.3.4 (bits2octets) reduces the hash mod n first. libsecp256k1 has done so since 0.2.0. So for a hash >= n the framework's signature differs from libsecp256k1's, though it is still valid.

This is a small, correct fix with a test. The test checks two signatures computed with libsecp256k1, one of them for a hash >= n, and fails without the fix. The change has no practical effect on current tests: the only caller, `feature_taproot.py`, signs double-SHA256 sighashes, which are >= n with probability about 2^-128. If reviewers see no benefit, feel free to close it.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: wallet: bound pending MuSig2 sessions
pulls.body:
The wallet keeps the secret nonce of every unfinished MuSig2 session in locked memory for as long as the wallet is loaded. A nonce is removed only when its session makes a partial signature, so each session that stops before that leaves 144 bytes of locked memory behind, with no bound on how many.

I keep at most 32768 sessions per wallet and drop the oldest first. The nonces move from each descriptor to the wallet, because every descriptor that can sign for our key in a `musig()` starts sessions, and each one kept its own. A dropped nonce is never reused. If no participant has added a partial signature for that MuSig2 key yet, removing our pubnonce and running round 1 again restarts the session; otherwise all participants restart the round with new nonces. A release note says so. A standard transaction has at most 1738 signed Taproot inputs, so the limit allows 18 sessions per input, enough for any tree of up to 6 signers with a MuSig2 key path and one MuSig2 leaf per k-of-n subset. At the limit a wallet's nonces use 4.5 MiB of locked memory. Unit tests fill the limit and start one more session through the same descriptor and through another one of the same wallet; they fail without the change.
